items.title: Sailing along a constant compass bearing draws a spiral around the pole
items.claim: A 'rhumb line' (loxodrome) is a path that crosses every meridian at the same angle — what you sail if you hold a constant compass course. Except for due east/west (the equator) or due north/south, a rhumb line spirals around the pole, eventually reaching it after infinite winding.
items.prompt: Why doesn't a constant bearing give a great circle?

options.text: Great circles change bearing as you traverse them (except along the equator or meridians); to maintain a constant compass bearing, you must follow a different curve that spirals — the loxodrome
It only happens near the pole

items.reveal:
A loxodrome (rhumb line) is the curve that intersects all meridians at the same angle. On a sphere, this is an equiangular spiral.

For any constant bearing not aligned with the equator or a meridian, the path spirals around the pole. The length to reach the pole is finite (the spiral converges) but the number of windings is infinite.

On a Mercator projection, rhumb lines appear as straight lines — this is the property Mercator designed his projection for in 1569. Hold a ruler against a Mercator chart and you have a constant compass bearing course.

Great circles, by contrast, appear as curves on Mercator maps, generally bowed toward the nearer pole. Modern aviation uses great-circle routes; old-school open-ocean sailing used rhumb lines (easier to navigate without constant heading recalculation).

In practice: long-distance navigation often combines them — fly an approximate great circle, but compute waypoints at intervals (e.g., every 5 degrees of longitude) and sail rhumb lines between waypoints. This is 'composite sailing'.

The loxodrome was first studied by the Portuguese navigator Pedro Nunes (1537). It contributed to the systematic mathematisation of navigation in the Age of Discovery.
items.why: Compasses point to magnetic north. Holding a constant bearing draws a curve that no Euclidean intuition prepares you for — and the difference between loxodrome and great circle has shaped maps, navigation, and naval strategy for centuries.

items.title: The sum of all positive integers equals minus one twelfth
items.claim: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + ... = -1/12. This obviously fails as a normal sum (it diverges to infinity). But it is the value of the Riemann zeta function analytically continued to s = -1, and it shows up in physics (Casimir effect, string theory).
items.prompt: How does an obviously divergent sum get a finite value?

options.text: Analytic continuation extends a function defined on one domain (where the series converges) to a larger domain (where the series doesn't); zeta(-1) is well-defined as a function value even though the corresponding series diverges
Negative numbers were added without permission

items.reveal_title: Ramanujan, Hardy, and the strange identity
items.reveal:
Srinivasa Ramanujan wrote to Hardy in 1913 claiming results like 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ... = -1/12. Hardy initially thought Ramanujan must be a crank — until he checked.

The Riemann zeta function is defined by zeta(s) = sum from n=1 to infinity of 1/n to the power s, but only when the real part of s exceeds 1. The function extends analytically to the whole complex plane (except a pole at s = 1). At s = -1, zeta(-1) = -1/12.

If you formally substitute s = -1 into the series, you get 1 + 2 + 3 + ... The series doesn't converge there — but the function it defined still has a value, just by a different (analytic continuation) method.

In quantum field theory, the same -1/12 appears. The Casimir force calculation involves summing zero-point energies of standing waves; this sum diverges, but the physical answer obtained by zeta regularisation matches experiment.

The identity is not casually 'true' as arithmetic. It's true as the value of a specific extension of the zeta function — and that extension happens to give physically correct predictions.
items.why: Treating divergent sums as if they have finite values seems like a trick — but in the right framework, analytic continuation gives them precise meanings that physics turns out to use.

items.title: Knowing the equations exactly doesn't let you predict the weather
items.claim: The atmosphere obeys Newton's laws, well-known fluid dynamics, well-known thermodynamics. Knowing all the equations doesn't let us predict beyond about 10 to 14 days. The system is deterministic but unpredictable.
items.prompt: How can determinism coexist with unpredictability?

options.text: In chaotic systems, infinitesimally different initial conditions diverge exponentially over time; predicting day 20 requires knowing today's conditions to a precision beyond physical measurement

items.reveal:
Edward Lorenz, simulating weather on a vacuum-tube computer in 1961, restarted a calculation from intermediate data printed to 3 decimal places. The internal precision was 6 places. The truncated and full simulations diverged completely within a simulated month.

He published the result in 1963 with a simplified 3-equation model showing strange attractor dynamics. His 1972 talk title — 'Does the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas?' — gave us the butterfly effect.

The key insight: any uncertainty in initial conditions doubles every few days in the atmosphere. After 10 doublings — about 2 to 3 weeks — uncertainty in tiny details has grown to dominate the whole forecast.

Ensemble weather forecasting (running many simulations from slightly perturbed starts) addresses this by giving a probability distribution rather than a single prediction.
items.why: Determinism is conflated with predictability. Lorenz showed they are different: the equations may be exact and the system may still be unpredictable in practice, because small errors grow exponentially.
